speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Act provides for the extradition of fugitives, in other words, the surrender of a fugitive by one state to another in which he or she is liable to be prosecuted or punished.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is invoked when the fugitive flees from the state that he or she has been charged or sentenced to another state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As then-Minister for Law and National Development, Mr EW Barker, said when the Act was first passed in Parliament in 1968 – "It is not in states' interest to afford refuge to criminals from other countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the contrary, it is in states' interests to return fugitives for trial and punishment to the state in which the offence was committed or in which the criminal was convicted." It is, therefore, important for us to review the Act to ensure that our extradition framework remains robust.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst many of the concepts in the Act remain relevant and applicable today, apart from minor amendments in 1970 and 1998, the Act has remained largely unchanged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry conducted an extensive comparative study of various common law and civil law jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These jurisdictions include Australia, Brunei, Canada, Malaysia, France, Japan and the US, amongst others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To keep in pace with current needs, it is timely to introduce modern concepts, taking into account global developments and international practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are five key amendments in this Bill – two areas of substantive reform and three areas of procedural reform.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are several other amendments in the Bill which are technical or consequential in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will explain a few of the more material amendments but the Explanatory Note to the Bill describes in some detail the nature of the various provisions in the Bill and I will not elaborate on all of them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is no general obligation under international law to surrender a fugitive to a foreign state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is due to the principle of state sovereignty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A mutual arrangement or treaty between states is usually required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, Singapore can extradite: (a) Fugitives to 40 declared Commonwealth territories under the London Scheme for Extradition within the Commonwealth, and I will refer to this as the London Scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The territories within the Commonwealth include Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: (b) Singapore can also extradite fugitives to Germany, the US and Hong Kong – jurisdictions with which an extradition treaty or agreement is in force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: (c) State parties to multilateral treaties which Singapore is a party to – such as the International Convention against the Taking of Hostages and the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: (d) Finally, Malaysia and Brunei – based on the reciprocal arrangements for the endorsement of arrest warrants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also signed a treaty with Indonesia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When it enters into force, we will be able to extradite fugitives to and from Indonesia on the terms as set out in that treaty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The proposed amendments seek to strike the right balance between international cooperation and individual liberty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a responsible global citizen, we must contribute to the fight against crime, by empowering our authorities to facilitate extradition requests, where justified.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, recognising that extradition is a coercive process, we must also ensure that there are robust safeguards in place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And this Bill seeks to introduce amendments that would enhance: (a) our ability to facilitate extradition requests; and (b) the protection for persons who are wanted by foreign jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will adopt a threshold approach for determining whether an offence is extraditable, also known as an "extradition offence".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This would be subject to an exclusionary list.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, the Act provides for a positive list approach, where only offences which are on the list would be extraditable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the time the Act was first introduced, the list approach was the norm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The offences listed in our Act were aligned with the negotiated approach in the 1966 London Scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, since that time, international practice is moving away from the list approach in favour of the threshold approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, the London Scheme itself was amended to adopt a threshold approach in 2002.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will exclude some offences which, despite crossing that threshold, are regulatory in nature, and do not warrant the use of state resources for extradition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are reflected in the list of excluded offences in the new First Schedule to the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members can have a look at the Schedule and will see offences, such as the prohibition of import or transhipment of fresh fruits and vegetables without a licence under the Control of Plants Act 1993.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Another example – the production of false evidence on the register of trademarks under the Trade Marks Act 1998 and some forms of building control offences or of that nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The threshold approach will make it easier to determine when an offence is extraditable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We do not expect this amendment to result in an undue increase in incoming extradition requests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: From our experience, our extradition partners have made requests in respect of relatively serious offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The principle of dual criminality, which requires that extraditable offences be punishable under the laws of both Singapore and the requesting state, will also be preserved in this Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we are expanding the safeguards under which a fugitive's extradition may be refused, a point which I will touch on in a moment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The second substantive reform deals with the expansion of restrictions on surrender.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are seeking to update and expand restrictions on the surrender of fugitives in the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are referred to as restrictions on surrender and there are several restrictions under the current Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, where the fugitive was convicted in his or her absence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Conviction in the fugitive's absence is, generally, considered a denial of natural justice and leaves the fugitive unable to contest allegations against him or her.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This restriction is consistent with our domestic legislation, section 156 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 (CPC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This mandatory restriction, however, does not apply if the fugitive had deliberately absented himself or herself, or if there is an opportunity for retrial.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where the prosecution of the fugitive is barred in the requesting state by its limitation period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, if the limitation period for the prosecution of an offence is 15 years, and the extradition of the fugitive is requested 20 years after the offence was committed, then the requesting state would not be able to prosecute the fugitive by virtue of its own limitation period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That being the case, it would not be appropriate for Singapore to facilitate that extradition, since the requesting state would not be able to prosecute the fugitive upon his or her return.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The restrictions also apply where the offence committed is for a military offence which is not punishable under criminal law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a tool in international criminal cooperation, extradition is meant to combat crimes, as opposed to disciplinary offences within a military organisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is also consistent with the London Scheme, as well as the approach which we have taken under our Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act 2000 (MACMA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The next category is where the remaining imprisonment term for the fugitive is de minimus in nature.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This applies to a fugitive who has been convicted and sentenced for a crime in the requesting state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This does not apply to a fugitive who has been charged with but not yet convicted and sentenced in the requesting state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is the default minimal remaining imprisonment term, unless otherwise stated in the relevant extradition treaty between Singapore and the requesting state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have introduced this restriction as it may not be appropriate to extradite a fugitive where the remaining imprisonment term may be shorter than the time required to complete the extradition process itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, however, is a discretionary restriction because there may be instances where surrender of the fugitive is, nevertheless, warranted, despite having met the requirement for the discretionary restriction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The updated and expanded restrictions on surrender will provide more robust safeguards for individuals who are subjects of extradition requests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill introduces a mechanism for fugitives to consent to their extradition under the new sections 16 and 21.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, the Act does not allow a fugitive to consent to extradition and all fugitives must undergo the full extradition proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This leads to cases where extradition proceedings continue even though the fugitive has indicated that he or she would not contest the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further, when a Magistrate has committed a fugitive to be surrendered to the requesting state, the fugitive cannot be surrendered until 15 days have elapsed since the committal order, even if the fugitive does not intend to apply for an order for review of the Magistrate's order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A fugitive may also waive his or her right to apply for a review of the Magistrate's order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This saves state resources and prevents the fugitive from being detained longer than necessary in Singapore as there is no need for a full extradition hearing to be carried out if there is consent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The fugitive will then be surrendered as soon as practicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court has to ascertain that the fugitive's consent is voluntary and inform the fugitive of the consequences of that consent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A specialty undertaking would be obtained from the requesting state, unless the fugitive waives such an undertaking.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that the fugitive will only be prosecuted for the offences stated in the extradition request, and not for additional offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will ensure the fugitive does not lose an important protection simply because he or she consents to extradition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It also ensures the fugitive understands the full scope of offences for which he or she will be prosecuted for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will align Singapore with many other jurisdictions, such as Australia, Canada, Germany, Malaysia, New Zealand, the UK and the US, that allow fugitives to consent to their extradition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, I will touch on amendments which seek to centralise review procedures for extradition proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill consolidates the applicable procedures for review of a Magistrate's order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: After a fugitive is apprehended, a Magistrate will hear evidence as to whether the fugitive ought to be committed to prison to await surrender to the requesting state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Magistrate will then make an order to either commit or discharge the fugitive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A fugitive who has been ordered to be detained may apply for an order for review of detention under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, it incorporates the fugitive's right to apply to the High Court under CPC for an order for review of detention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A review of a Magistrate's order does not require permission of the Court and can be on a question of fact or law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The High Court may make any order or direction as it thinks fit upon the review, and the High Court’s decision is final.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to ensure that there will be finality to the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have provided for the possibility of the fugitive being released on bail pending the determination of the High Court's review of the Attorney-General's application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This balances the rights of the individual with the state's international obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The new section 18 provides that either party may refer a question of law of public interest which arose during a review by the High Court to the Court of Appeal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is based on section 397 of CPC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The ability of the Attorney-General to apply for a review of an order to release the fugitive will also remove the need to process extradition applications afresh or re-arrest the fugitive following his or her discharge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This aligns Singapore's extradition framework with international practice and the provisions of the London Scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, let me touch on the amendments which update evidential procedures for extradition proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In deciding whether a fugitive should be committed to await extradition to the requesting state, the Court must consider whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant the extradition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Usually, this evidence is presented by way of affidavits, which can sometimes be voluminous.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A record of the case summarises the evidence acquired by a requesting state or territory in support of its extradition request.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The record of the case must be certified by a judicial or prosecuting authority of the requesting state, who must state that the evidence summarised or contained in the record of the case is available to be produced at the person's trial and sufficient under the law of the requesting state to justify prosecution of the person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court retains discretion in determining the weight to be given to the evidence admitted by way of a record of the case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The record of the case is only permissible if there is a treaty or arrangement allowing for such mechanism to be used.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ensures that there will be reciprocity between Singapore and its extradition partner, and that Singapore will also receive similar treatment when making the extradition request to the foreign party.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The record of the case mechanism facilitates extradition proceedings by simplifying procedures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is aligned with international practice and is employed by some of our extradition partners, such as Canada and New Zealand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have clarified that the bail and bond provisions under CPC apply with certain modifications to persons released on bail or bond under the Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also codified the powers of an authorised officer under the Act to search and seize property in the possession of the fugitive at the time of his or her arrest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such property would be confined to physical items.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This makes the Act self-contained by housing all the extradition offences, which are currently disparate, under a single piece of legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These other statutes implement and give effect to the various multilateral conventions which Singapore is party to, including extradition provisions contained in conventions, such as the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act 2002, which implements Singapore's obligations under the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism; and the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act 2007, which implements our obligations under the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These frameworks were previously separate due to the historical fact that the provisions were derived from the Extradition Act 1870 for foreign states and the Fugitive Offenders Act 1881 for declared Commonwealth territories respectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over time, the relevant considerations and safeguards applied similarly across foreign states or Commonwealth territories, regardless of wherefrom the request was made.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have, therefore, streamlined and combined the frameworks for clarity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We recognise that this Part provides a simple and expeditious procedure that has worked well in the past and in practice for the return of fugitive offenders from Singapore to Malaysia and also vice versa.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The amendments in this Bill form a comprehensive update to the Act, taking into account developments in international practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Extradition is an essential component of international law enforcement and plays a key role in upholding the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For legal practitioners and Government officers in the know, this is not an easy task.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As will be seen from my speech, Singapore’s extradition framework is shaped by Singapore’s complex constitutional history and special relationship with several of our neighbouring states.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, therefore, appreciate the difficulties our legislative drafters faced in their attempt to simplify and modernise the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If they were to draft this Act from a clean slate, I suspect it would have been a much easier task to do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will cover five areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I seek clarification on the definition of “foreign state” that is proposed in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I seek clarification on two procedural issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are the need to retain the Magistrate’s independent jurisdiction to issue warrants of apprehension against fugitives, instead of doing so only when authorised by the Minister; and the absence of a provision that specifies who can make the applications to invoke the powers of the Court under the Extradition Act to issue warrants for apprehension of fugitives and commit the fugitive to be surrendered to the authorities of the requesting state.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I seek a short clarification on how the threshold approach to determining an extraditable offence would apply in situations where the underlying treaty between Singapore and the foreign country specifies extraditable offences based on categories of offences listed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fourth, I seek a clarification on the issue of alignment between this Act and the existing extradition framework dealing with Malaysia and Brunei.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the first area, I note that it is proposed that the definition of what constitutes a “foreign state” in the current Act be retained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This includes a foreign state which had an extradition treaty with the British Empire at the time when Singapore was part of it, unless the Minister stipulates otherwise in a gazette notification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is how the 1931 extradition treaty between the US and Singapore came into being.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was entered into between the US and UK when Singapore was a British colony.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore’s right to this extradition arose in her capacity as the successor by operation of law which was subsequently recognised by exchange of letters between the respective governments of the states in 1969.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result of this definition, there remains uncertainty as to which other foreign states may be held to be able to invoke the extradition processes under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that Prof S Jayakumar, as an academic, made in 1970 in his published article entitled “Singapore and State Succession”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His point was echoed by NUS law lecturer, Ms Janice Brabyn, in her 1985 published article entitled, “Extradition in Singapore and Malaysia”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They include Austria, Denmark, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Luxembourg and Switzerland.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will promote certainty and remove the chance of any dispute on this issue arising in Court, something that Prof Jayakumar was concerned about in his article.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said: “The problem could arise in proceedings to extradite a fugitive to a foreign state on the basis of a pre-Independence Treaty concluded by the UK with that foreign state.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fugitive might challenge the proceedings on the ground that the extradition treaty is not one which 'extends to and is binding on Singapore'.” May I ask the hon Minister why he is proposing to still retain the original definition of “Foreign State” in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, I wonder if the Minister would consider listing them in a schedule to the Act or by way of subsidiary legislation in the near future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the second area, in this Bill, it is proposed that two current mechanisms to commence extradition proceedings in Singapore be retained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, a Magistrate may, by authorisation of the Minister through a notice, issue a warrant of apprehension of a fugitive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, the Magistrate may issue a same warrant through an application made directly to him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question is: why give the Magistrate the power to issue a warrant independently?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be better to just require any state which wishes to invoke the Extradition Act to make a requisition first to the Minister or the Attorney-General’s Chambers on behalf of the Government through diplomatic channels?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would imagine this is the case for most cases, if not for all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, it would be preferable for the Minister, or if it is perceived that there is a need to create extra bandwidth, a person or committee appointed by the Minister, to act as a filter to determine the “bona fides” of the requesting state.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not an easily justiciable question that a Court can decide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, it is specifically provided in the proposed section 12(4) of the Bill that the Minister may direct a warrant issued by the Magistrate without the authorisation of the Minister to be cancelled.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To be fair, this is something which is already in place under the Act now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the policy intent is for the Minister to be satisfied there is ground to initiate or proceed with extradition proceedings, would it not be better to altogether remove the Magistrate’s jurisdiction to issue warrants against fugitives on his own?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This leads me to the next question as to who can make applications to invoke the powers of the Court under the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some provisions in the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, or MACMA, as it is often referred to, overlap in purpose with the provisions of the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In both cases, Singapore is being asked to assist foreign states in criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MACMA deals with evidence needed for overseas criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Extradition Act deals with persons accused or convicted of crime overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under section 22 of MACMA, it is specifically provided that it is the Attorney-General (AG) or a person duly appointed by the AG who may apply to the Court for production orders on behalf of the foreign country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on my checks, there is no equivalent section in the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Attorney-General’s role under the Act is specified only from the point after an order is made by the Magistrate on application for extradition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, he may make an application for a review of the order by the General Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do accept, in practice, officers of the AGC usually make the applications under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But having regard to the point I made about the general jurisdiction of the Magistrate to issue warrants of apprehension against fugitives and the fact that the definition of “Foreign States” may be more expansive than currently thought, it seems to me open for a party which has interest in a matter to apply and invoke the general jurisdiction of the Court, thereby bypassing AGC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move to the third area, which is the proposed implementation of the threshold approach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the hon Minister explained, this means that the offences which are punished by a maximum of two years' imprisonment would automatically be considered extradition offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a shift from the current model which maintains a list of offences which will require an update periodically.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I must point out we are enabled to make this move now because there has been, in the recent past, a massive rationalisation exercise to ensure that the maximum sentences for offences have been updated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This move is also calibrated in that the double criminality principle, requiring the offences to be punishable by a maximum punishment of more than two years’ imprisonment in both the requesting and requested states, is retained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the treaty between the US and Singapore, there are 27 categories of offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the US be able to extradite from Singapore a fugitive wanted for an offence that is not in the list but satisfies the threshold requirements?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The next area I wish to deal with concerns Singapore’s special extradition arrangements with Malaysia and Brunei.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This involves a considerably simplified process when it comes to extraditing a person in Singapore accused or convicted of an offence under the laws of Malaysia and Brunei.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is laid down in just one section of the Criminal Procedure Code, section 121, which has five subsections, and all in one page.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under this arrangement, which, by the way, applies to Singapore reciprocally, too, when a warrant is issued by a Malaysian or Brunei Court, the Singapore Court may just endorse the said warrant and, thereafter, it is treated as a warrant issued by a Singapore Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This simplified process reflects the special relationship between Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei and I fully support it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Drawing from my personal experience as a former Police officer, I recall in the early 1990s, I was investigating a case of a girl alleged to have been kidnapped from lawful guardianship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The father of the girl provided information that the accused and his daughter were likely to be in Ulu Tiram, Johor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Within a matter of hours, a Malaysian police officer escorted my colleagues and I to the location identified by the father to look for the accused and the victim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These special arrangements enable Police officers to pursue criminals even across borders as quickly as possible in an effort to bring them to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the Bill, I note that in the proposed Part 6, it deals only with the arrangement with Malaysia substantially as it is set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One of the objectives of the Bill, as I understand, is to collate extradition offences stated in other pieces of legislation into the proposed Fourth Schedule of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In light of that intent, may I please ask why is it not felt that there is a part under the Act to deal with the special arrangement with Brunei?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is he also to have regard to the requirements in Part 6 of the Extradition Act?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I ask this because there is no reference in the provisions set out in the Extradition Act and CPC to each other, even though the subject matter is the same.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My final area deals with the applicability of Singapore’s local public interest to extradition applications here and possible clashes with the policy of other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Article 11 of our Constitution prohibits a person from being punished for an act or omission which is not punishable by law when it was done.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This protection against retrospective criminal laws, however, does not apply universally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, Pakistan’s Ehtesab Act 1997, which focuses on corruption by politicians and public officers, has retrospective effect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us consider a case of a country seeking to extradite a fugitive from Singapore for an offence of bribery which satisfies all the proposed criteria set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does a Singapore Court have a discretion, nonetheless, not to order an order which goes against Singapore’s local public interest?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or is the Court supposed to ignore Singapore’s local public interest altogether?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it be better to have reserved for the Singapore Court a residual discretion to take action that it deems fit, depending on the circumstances of the case?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But based on my consideration of the proposed clause, this clause is not intended to apply to Singapore’s public interest in the matter under consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had argued that there should be clarity on the identity of foreign states with whom Singapore has extradition treaties, given the complexities of her constitutional history.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I argued that, for Malaysia and Brunei, with whom we have special extradition arrangements, there should be better alignment with this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggested that the AG be specifically appointed to invoke all the powers under the Act from the outset and not just from the point of review of an order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, the proposals I have made are in line with the aims of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our role as legislators involves calibration of matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Careful calibration is needed to achieve certainty, the judicious use of our state and judicial resources and ensuring that Singapore truly fulfils its role as a responsible global citizen in the arena of extradition of fugitives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further stated then that the amendments would "Cement Singapore's role as a responsible global citizen".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similar arrangements exist with Brunei as well, and I understand that these have worked well overall.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, apart from Malaysia and Brunei, the Bill is proposing notable changes to the existing framework for extradition to and from declared Commonwealth countries and foreign states.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, I find the changes in the Bill to be an improvement, being rational and less technical than the current scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I agree with the removal of the distinct parts of the Act covering declared Commonwealth countries and other foreign states in favour of many common provisions that will apply to all treaty countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The other change I support is the threshold approach to determine what offences are extraditable instead of the current scheme of looking at a positive list of extraditable crimes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also a new provision to enable the fugitive to consent to extradition, saving time and cost.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have some queries and an observation to make.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My speech today will cover whether the Government's general approach to extradition has changed; clarifications on safeguards for persons in Singapore against unjustifiable extradition requests; and, finally, an observation about why compromises to secure extradition are justifiable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, whether there has been any change in the Government's general approach to extradition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At a general level, I would like to clarify whether this Bill is a signal that the Government is changing its traditional somewhat guarded approach towards entering extradition treaties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Four years ago, during MinLaw's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, I had raised the COS cut on extradition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The specific case used for discussion was that of Mr David Roach who had committed robbery at a bank at Holland Village.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Members may recall that Mr Roach could not be extradited to Singapore when he was in nearby Thailand, but only when he travelled through London on the way back to his home country, Canada.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The then-Senior Minister of State for Law, Ms Indranee Rajah, explained at the COS the Government's general approach to extradition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She said that while the Government was open to entering new extradition treaties, such negotiations were complex.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Relevant considerations included whether such an arrangement would be mutually beneficial and whether any divergence in legal systems could be rationalised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She also highlighted that if there were inadequate protections, there would be risks to people in Singapore, including our citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, safeguards for persons in Singapore, including citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In terms of safeguards against unjustified extradition requests, the Bill provides more protections by enhancing the restrictions on the surrender of persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 6 of the Bill, the new sections 8 to 10 set out the restrictions on the surrender of persons in Singapore to other countries, as well as restrictions on the Minister's powers to authorise the apprehension of fugitives in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are, overall, more safeguards in this Bill than currently, such as not extraditing someone if he was convicted in a foreign state in his absence, or if the offence alleged is one which, under Singapore law, would only be an offence under military law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For extradition from Malaysia and Brunei, my understanding is that there is no time bar.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hence, we read of persons wanted in Singapore who are apprehended in Malaysia three or four decades after the incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for countries other than Malaysia and Brunei, some protections already exist in the current Act for the Minister to refuse extradition to Commonwealth countries if there has been a passage of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Historically, we know that there has been strong interest from Indonesia to conclude a treaty with Singapore after the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997 to 1998.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Shortly thereafter, in 1999, then Law Minister, Prof S Jayakumar, told Parliament that the Indonesians had made a request for such a treaty which Singapore was considering.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is widely known that the Indonesian government wishes to prosecute Indonesians who may have embezzled millions of dollars during the crisis and fled here thereafter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I can only assume that some of those who came to Singapore may have acquired Singapore citizenship by now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am still unclear about how this would operate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Eighteen years prior to this year would bring us back to the year 2004.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister explain how this year's treaty would facilitate the extradition of fugitives who fled here after the Asian Financial Crisis after a passage of 24 years?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not knowledgeable about the requirements of Indonesian law and the Government's clarification of this will be useful for public understanding.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some members of the public did not find this to be a fair outcome as Mr Roach did not suffer the full punishment ordered by the Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A similar situation had arisen in the earlier case of Mr Michael McCrae, who was extradited from Australia in 2005, to face trial here for murder, which carried the death penalty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that case, the Singapore Government also had to assure the Australian government that the fugitive would not face the death penalty in order to secure his extradition to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, a fundamental principle of sovereignty is that countries need not concern themselves with offences committed in other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, going after criminals on behalf of another country requires time and expense and burdens the country's legal system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If a country has entered an agreement for mutual extradition, it is entitled to set qualifications to its obligations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This reality is, no doubt, a compromise on certain principles, but it is, certainly, better than letting offenders escape justice altogether.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It reduces bureaucracy for a whole slew of parties, including individuals facing possible extradition, jurisdictions requesting the extradition, and judges making decisions on extradition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the surrender of persons to declared Commonwealth territories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, section 28 categorises offences against the life of a political figure and their immediate family as non-political offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the significance of this specific carve-out?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And why, in general, do additional restrictions apply in cases where Commonwealth territories are the ones requesting the extradition?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point today is about Ministerial discretion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Multiple sections in the Bill empower the Minister to exercise his discretion to decide for or against extradition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In section 29, for instance, the Minister may refuse to extradite a person to a Commonwealth territory in multiple cases, including when a person's conviction was obtained in their absence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In section 8(8), the Minister may refuse to extradite a person to a foreign state when their remaining sentence is minimal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For section 8(8), when might we choose to extradite someone even though their remaining sentence is minimal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would seem to run against the intent of the subsection, which is to empower the Government to save resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last point is about the use of summarised evidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what mechanisms are in place to ensure that this summary of evidence is sufficient for the Minister to make the required determination under the Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What mechanisms are in place to ensure this summary is sufficient for the Minister to ascertain if such substantial grounds exist?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I support the streamlining of provisions on extradition requests for declared Commonwealth countries and other non-Commonwealth foreign states into a single framework and also the enhancement of the review procedures for extradition proceedings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also welcome the introduction of the threshold approach for determining the extradition offences, which is a major change to the existing list approach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This approach will make for easier applicability and also bring us in line with countries like the UK, Australia, Canada and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill expands also on the restrictions on surrender.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In other words, the Bill expands on the list of excluded offences or circumstances which preclude extradition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This also modernises our approach in this respect, adding to the circumstances seen in many extradition treaties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And so, it should not extend to offences which, if under the requesting country's military laws, the acts leading to the offences might not have come within our SAF Act offences but under another statute, for example, our Enlistment Act offences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, I welcome the new provisions under this Bill allowing a fugitive to consent to extradition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister whether the new requirements on search and seizure under clause 15, which provides for seizure of anything in the possession or control of a fugitive that may be material as evidence, will cover proceeds of fraud or offences relating to fraud, corruption or graft.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill also introduces a record of the case mechanism.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is supposed to simplify existing requirements and procedures for the admission of evidence to support an application for extradition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a record of the case summarises the evidence presented by a requesting state or is to be certified by a judicial or prosecuting authority.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, I have a point of clarification on clause 16(8)(c).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This clause provides that pursuant to sub-clauses 8(a) to (c), the Magistrate is to commit the person to await the warrant of the Minister for the surrender but otherwise, subject to section 17, is to order that person be released.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, before I close, I actually wanted to ask the Minister, given the changes to our extradition laws under this Bill and including the provision allowing consent by fugitives, does the Government expect that the amended law will result in an increased number of people being now eligible for extradition for offences committed in home countries in the past.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And if I heard the Minister correctly, I think the indication is no.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On a related note, I would also like to ask the Minister whether following the recent extradition treaty with Indonesia, does the Government expect to handle a spike in the number of fugitives being extradited and also whether it is making plans to handle such an increase in volume.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, I have heard the Members' comments and some questions as to its operations and processes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But there has been overall support and I will address those questions in turn as best as I can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why we have proposed to retain the definition of "foreign state" in the Extradition Act and whether we could consider listing the foreign states in a Schedule in the Act or by way of subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, of course, making the changes and retaining those that continue to work well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The definition of "foreign state" is one such instance which continues to work well for our present purposes, with slight adjustments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The definitions that we have retained had been updated previously in 1998.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai mentioned that the definition of "foreign state" includes a foreign state which had a treaty with the British Empire at the time when Singapore was part of it and that this could cause uncertainty as to which foreign states may be held to be able to invoke the extradition processes under the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has been previously clarified in this House that whilst it is true that before Singapore's Independence, there were extradition treaties entered into by the United Kingdom and other foreign countries in which Singapore was listed in the scope of operations of these treaties, it does not follow that, today, all those arrangements automatically apply to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, these pre-Independence treaties will only apply where the Government has considered that these treaties are binding on Singapore and where we have published this in subsidiary legislation, as Mr Murali Pillai has suggested.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The relevant treaties are published as subsidiary legislation in the Federal Republic of Germany (Extradition) Order in Council and the United States of America (Extradition) Order in Council.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for clarification as to why there are special restrictions on surrender to declared Commonwealth territories and also why, in general, do additional restrictions apply in cases where Commonwealth countries request extradition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has also asked about the significance of section 28, which provides that offences against the life or a person of a political figure or a member of the political figure's immediate family, are not offences of a political character.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Act contains an existing restriction on surrender in section 9(1), where a fugitive is not liable to be surrendered if the offence is of a political character.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The fugitive may be extradited in such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This specific carve-out to the restriction on surrender is adapted from clause 12(2)(a) of the London Scheme, which, as I earlier mentioned, would only apply for declared Commonwealth territories.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For completeness, the Member also observed that there are additional restrictions that apply to Commonwealth territories and not to foreign states.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These additional restrictions are where the offence was committed outside the requesting state and Singapore and is not an extraterritorial offence under the law of the requesting state; and where the person has become immune from prosecution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason that these additional restrictions apply for declared Commonwealth territories is because these are aligned with the London Scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, it is not the case that where a request of such a nature is made by a non-Commonwealth territory, that such a carve-out to the restriction on surrender for offences of a political character would never apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For all foreign states and territories that are not part of the Commonwealth, the bilateral or multilateral treaty in place would be the primary source of our international obligations to each other in relation to extradition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this also addresses Ms Sylvia Lim's point about what we do with the new treaties, including that with Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of our bilateral and multilateral treaties contain a similar provision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, I pointed out earlier that the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings makes it clear that a terrorist bombing offence is not an offence of a political character.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore would similarly be obliged not to restrict the surrender of a fugitive to the foreign state or territory in the event the offence was the bombing of a political figure's residence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On this note, this brings me to Mr Murali Pillai's query on how the shift to the threshold approach for extraditable offences would be reconciled with our bilateral treaties which adopt the list approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think several Members also touched on the question of how you might reconcile this in the context of having a treaty and also the impact that this Bill might or might not have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned that Singapore's existing extradition treaties would be the primary source for our international obligations to foreign states and territories.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where applicable, however, the threshold approach could, in some cases, widen the scope of extraditable offences under our bilateral treaties and arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, this is not the case for the example which Mr Murali Pillai cited vis-a-vis our bilateral treaty with the US.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would respect the fundamental principle in international law that the ambit of the treaty governs the obligations between the states.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether we could share scenarios on how the Ministerial discretion is meant to be exercised in deciding to accede to or reject an extradition request.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan also touched on a question of when the Magistrate might order the release of the fugitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To deal with this point – for instance, when would the Minister choose to extradite a fugitive even when his or her remaining imprisonment term is minimal – I mentioned earlier in my opening speech that there may be instances where the surrender of the fugitive is, nevertheless, warranted, even if the remaining imprisonment term might be minimal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, there might be significant public interest in the requesting state or territory for the return of that fugitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in such a scenario, we might decide to accede to the extradition request even if the requirement for the discretionary restriction has been met.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had explained earlier that the record of the case mechanism simplifies the procedure for admission of evidence to justify the extradition of a fugitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers and my Ministry will ensure that every extradition request is sufficiently substantiated with such evidence before we accede to the extradition request and commence committal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the committal proceedings before a Magistrate, the Magistrate would similarly need to be satisfied of the prima facie evidence requirement, before the person can be committed to prison to await their surrender to the requesting state.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng raised, as an example, the restrictions of the Minister's power to order a person's surrender if the Minister has substantial grounds for believing that the person would be prosecuted for reasons of race, religion, sex, ethnic origin, nationality or political opinion, and what mechanisms would be in place to ensure the summary of evidence is sufficient for the Minister to ascertain that such grounds exist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Generally, if there is reason to believe that a person is going to be discriminated against, or prosecuted along one of these discrimination grounds, then you are unlikely to find that the evidence submitted by the requesting state would detail this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the contrary, if there is a dearth of credible evidence in the extradition request justifying the commission of the alleged offence by the fugitive, this could form a basis and contribute to the grounds for the Minister's belief that the fugitive is being discriminated against or that one of the restrictions on surrender might apply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For completeness, we would add that Singapore has always required extradition requests from requesting states to also contain undertakings that the fugitive would not be prejudiced or otherwise punished for reason of race, religion, nationality or political opinions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This requirement will remain even with the introduction of the record of the case mechanism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why the Magistrate's power to issue warrants of arrest by a Notice by the Minister is being retained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Provisional arrest is the procedure that applies for urgent cases where a requested person is deemed to be a flight risk and there is insufficient time for the requesting state to prepare a full extradition request.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Murali Pillai mentioned, it is preferable, and, indeed, required, for any foreign state or territory to request the extradition of a fugitive through a formal request via diplomatic channels.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, there are, sometimes, cases where there is information that the fugitive is a flight risk and there is an urgent need to detain the fugitive to prevent him or her from fleeing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This allows Singapore to fulfil our international obligations under our treaties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such cases, where the overriding concern is to ensure the detention of the fugitive, the quickest way would be for the Magistrate to have the power to issue warrants of arrest without being authorised by a Notice by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Subsequently, a full extradition request must be submitted by the requesting state within a fixed number of days – the number of days depends itself on the terms of the treaty – and in any event, within a reasonable time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If, for example, the full extradition request and the supporting documents are not furnished by this time, or the documents are inadequate, or if any of the restrictions on surrender apply, the Minister can then direct the warrant to be cancelled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in this case, if after the initial arrest notice has been issued, it subsequently transpires that, upon review of the full set of extradition materials from the requesting state, these thresholds for committal are not met, then, in that scenario, the Minister can ask for the warrant to be cancelled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Dennis Tan's point, it is also in that scenario, that if the Magistrate is of the view that the threshold has not been reached, has not been crossed, then, in such a situation, the Magistrate can order a release.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether a Singapore Court has the discretion not to grant an order which goes against Singapore's public policy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having said that, in the event that the extradition request from the requesting state does, indeed, go against Singapore's public policy, the Minister can consider if this would fall within any of the restrictions on surrender, which have been enhanced in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these would be grounds on which to refuse the request for extradition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked who can make applications to invoke the powers of the Court under the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new section 50 provides that the Attorney-General may delegate to a public officer any of his or her powers under the Act and, in the Explanatory Statement, Members will see that it is elaborated upon that a public officer so empowered may act for the Attorney-General in Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the arrangements with Malaysia and Brunei and why the reciprocal arrangements with Brunei for the endorsement of arrest warrants are not included in the amended Act; and also asked about the legislative intent in relation to a Magistrate's powers under section 121 of the CPC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned earlier, aside from minor updating of the language, we have preserved the part on "Extradition To and From Malaysia".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is in Part 6 of the amended Act, by way of endorsement of arrest warrants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In practice, the Singapore and Malaysian authorities have largely relied on the section 121 of the CPC procedure, which, as Mr Murali Pillai mentioned, covers the same subject matter of the reciprocal endorsement of arrest warrants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about the special relationship with Malaysia and Brunei and I think his own experience shows that the officers on all three sides are aware of this and use this procedure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our operational agencies and their counterparts have some history and share a good working relationship on the basis of this established procedure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I had earlier alluded to, time is often of the essence in such matters where the fugitive is a flight-risk and familiarity with this working process, the good working relationship on the basis of section 121 of CPC is being retained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, since the section 121 CPC procedure is used more often in practice, we decided that it was not necessary to replicate this procedure for our arrangement with Brunei in the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Murali Pillai's ancillary question, a Magistrate's powers under section 121 of CPC are self-contained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the Magistrate would not need to have regard to Part 6 of the Extradition Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim raised, I think, two points and one comment, if I am not wrong, let me address them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, she asked if this represents a shift or a change in approach.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have always been desirous of looking at countries which have a common desire to work with us to strengthen comity, international collaboration on apprehension of criminals and bilateral cooperation in combating crime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to the extent that these arrangements are seen to be mutually beneficial, work for us and that we can overcome any issues related to the divergence of our respective legal systems, then we will be prepared to enter into treaties or arrangements with them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the second point concerning, I think it was restrictions, time-bar, if I am not wrong, if the position is such that the offence is time-barred in the sense that that foreign state is unable by reason of the time-bar to prosecute that fugitive in the foreign state, then we will not allow the extradition, on the basis that it would have been a futile extradition because you cannot prosecute that fugitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as to why 18 years, that was the request for that treaty and we acceded to 18 years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It could have been some other period of time but this was the consensus agreed upon with Indonesia concerning that treaty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked several other questions, I will just deal with them quickly before I end off.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As far as the point on military law is concerned, if the offence that the requesting state seeks to extradite a fugitive for is only a military offence, then such a scenario would not result in the extradition being permitted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the course of apprehending the fugitive, there are search and seizure provisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are, as I pointed out earlier, for physical items.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if this leads to other evidence, which suggests that there have been, as Mr Dennis Tan puts it, proceeds of a crime and so on, then the relevant investigations will entail on the evidence which follows such proceeds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Clarification for the Minister on his response regarding the extradition treaty with Indonesia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Basically, can I confirm that he is saying that as far as that is concerned, the terms of the bilateral treaty prevail over the Bill, in that sense?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I mean, it is between the two countries to agree.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is, as I mentioned in the past, the interest was always to pursue fugitives that fled Indonesia after the Asian Financial Crisis (AFC), which took place about 24 years ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I perhaps want to just clarify one point which I think the Member alluded to earlier in her speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When I said in my opening speech that there are some cases where you could widen, that might apply, for example, if your treaty is worded in a way which allows you to piggyback on what laws might be amended to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if your treaty says all offences which the state might now, or, at some stage, revise their statutes to cover, then, of course, in such a scenario, because it is a moving definition in the extradition treaty, it moves along with any amendments or enhancements that the state might offer, like in this case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if what was previously agreed is fixed at just one year imprisonment, you can only extradite for one year, then that would be binding on the parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if one says, it is for a period of time, or whatever you might choose at some stage to amend your laws to, then the treaty would follow that provision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in that scenario, it might widen, but, otherwise, the principal point is that the treaty obligations between the parties will be binding on the parties.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader, you might want to move for exempted business.
